source.title: Learning words in groups: fusion algebras, tensor ranks and grokking
source.authors: Maor Shutman; O. Louidor; Ran Tessler

record.file_problem: The supplied paper text is readable and includes the main text and appendices; no material file problem is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests grokking on algorithmic group-word tasks using two-layer perceptrons and a Hadamard surrogate, rather than reproducing the original modular-arithmetic setup and method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking trajectories for selected group-word settings and final-accuracy sweeps over widths and training fractions. The latter do not quantify the delay as training-set size changes. Terminal-weight analyses and theoretical rank bounds are also reported, but do not measure the temporal claims in V2 or identify whether runs implement the same algorithm in the sense of V6.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces grokking in a new setting, arbitrary group-word operations learned by a two-layer perceptron and a Hadamard surrogate, and shows train/test trajectories. That bears on V1. Its terminal-weight analysis across runs and models also touches V6. It does not re-run the original transformer and modular-addition method, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that two-layer networks can learn arbitrary group-word operations and exhibit grokking, and that the word tensor is typically low-rank. Networks find low-rank implementations aligned with basic self-conjugate representations, with the fusion structure pruning components. For plain multiplication, the networks implement Strassen-type efficient matrix multiplication. Under GD, the dynamics decouple into per-bsc subsystems.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses group-word operations, a two-layer perceptron and a Hadamard surrogate, rather than the original modular-arithmetic transformer setup. Most optimization experiments use pure gradient descent; some cited figure descriptions use AdamW.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that the fraction of held-out training examples permitting full generalization and the prominence of grokking depend on the group, word and model width; they note that these can be quite low in some cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Grokking trajectories (r2, r3, Appendix B.2/C.4) are obtained under plain gradient descent with MSE loss: no adaptive optimizer, no softmax, no explicit regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like delays can occur without adaptive optimizers, softmax numerics or explicit weight decay. This bears incidentally on V7 and V5 but is not a controlled test.

record.problems: The selected grokking trajectories are figure-only and provide no exact transition times. The paper does not give a controlled comparison of grokking delay across training-set sizes. The authors say effects depend on group, word and width; some settings have weak grokking or limited generalization.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix B.2 and C.4 contain additional train/test evolution plots, and Figure 9 left and Appendix C.3 contain final accuracy sweeps over groups, widths and training fractions. They were not extracted because the plots do not provide separately stated exact values or establish how optimization delay changes with training-set size.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. No delay-versus-training-fraction measurement is reported; the Figure 9 left and C.3 sweeps report only final accuracy.

Gradual circuit formation, later removal of memorization, and progress measures anticipating the jump. Only terminal weights are analysed; the bsc partitioning of rows during training is not timed against the test-accuracy jump.
All of it: no non-algorithmic data and no sweep of initialization scale or weight norm.
All of it: no LLM training.
All of it: no weight-decay manipulation, no critical dataset size, no ungrokking.
No controlled comparison of optimizers or numerics. Grokking is shown under plain GD with MSE loss, but not as a deliberate control.

missing.what: Final test accuracy versus training fraction and width, 20 runs with SD. Shows generalization breaks down below width- and group-dependent fractions.
Additional single-run train/test trajectories for several groups, words and fractions.
Run-to-run variation in terminal box covers and bsc-support, and differences between TLP and HD covers.
missing.locator: Appendix B.1 (Examples B.1, B.2); Sec. 4.6; Suggested General Principle 4(1)

missing.what: Author statement that grokking prominence depends on group, word and width and is sometimes quite low.

record.verdict_notes: Grokking is a secondary, figure-only demonstration here; the paper's focus is representation-theoretic analysis of terminal weights. None of the original sources is this paper. The V6 label rests on qualitative heatmap descriptions, not quantified algorithm comparisons.

versions.untested_parts: The study shows grokking on selected group-word settings, but does not quantify the optimization delay across training-set sizes or establish that smaller training sets require more optimization.

The paper studies terminal weight structure and optimization dynamics, but does not measure gradual formation of a generalizing circuit during grokking, later removal of memorizing components, or continuous progress measures anticipating the test-accuracy transition.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep testing a lazy-to-rich transition is reported.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is studied.
The paper does not test a low-norm or weight-decay efficiency account, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.

The paper does not identify and compare algorithms learned across runs. It reports variation in terminal weight configurations and says their bsc-support depends somehow on the initial assignment, but does not establish whether these configurations implement different algorithms.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities, floating-point softmax limits, or other numerical-artifact explanations is reported.
